title: Fireside chat on an agentic simulation: Race Condition
transcriptText:
[MUSIC PLAYING]
TOM GREENAWAY: Hi, everyone.
We're here for a Q&A session
about Race Condition, which
is a high-scale
agentic simulation
framework for planning
a marathon in Las Vegas
that we've built for the
developer keynote at Cloud Next.
I'm here with Casey West,
and I'm Tom Greenaway.
CASEY WEST: Yeah,
so we work together
to build the simulation software
itself, which is open-source.
And we've also produced
a developer solution.
But we thought it might
be interesting to have
a little bit of a discussion
about how it got built,
why we built it, some
of the considerations
that we had to put into it.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah, exactly.
I oversaw the frontend
development of the project,
and Casey took care of the
backend and oversaw that.
CASEY WEST: Maybe this
is a good opportunity
to introduce ourselves
a little bit.
Tom, what's your background, and
what put you in a good position
to work on the frontend?
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah,
so before Google,
I was an independent
game developer.
I made many mobile games, and
I've made many games in general
in my life.
And in Google, I was the web
games lead for the Chrome
Developer Relations team.
So I've always focused
on games in my career,
which is great for a 3D kind of
experience like Race Condition.
CASEY WEST: And my career is
mostly about backend software
development, large-scale
distributed systems,
and architecture.
So as we were thinking
about building a reference
architecture for a
large-scale distributed
system and especially
an agentic one,
my background was good for
working on the backend.
So it's always nice to be able
to come together with engineers
that have different backgrounds,
different levels of expertise.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah, absolutely.
Yeah, we have some
prepared questions.
CASEY WEST: We both have Qs
and we both have As, hopefully.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah, exactly.
So I'll ask you, Casey, tell
everyone about Race Condition.
CASEY WEST: Yeah, so we
mentioned a little bit,
but Race Condition is our name
for the reference architecture
that we put together that
runs the very real simulation
that hopefully you've seen on
the developer keynote at Next.
It's on YouTube.
We can put a link in the
description of this video.
But the idea was to build a
large-scale agentic system,
a real one that
could demonstrate
a lot of the capabilities
of some of our new platform
offerings.
So Google Cloud, of
course, is launching
a bunch of products at Next.
By the time you see this
video, that will have happened.
And a large number of those
products that we're really
focusing on are around what
we're calling Gemini Enterprise
Agent Platform, which is a
collection of platform services,
but also open-source standards,
frameworks, and protocols
that we put together
to help you build
large-scale agentic systems.
So we thought, let's build
one and show it to you.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah,
and you're actually
going to be at Cloud Next
in the developer keynote
with a bunch of other
Googlers showing off the demo.
And it's pretty cool
because on the frontend,
like on the client, it's this
3D recreation of Las Vegas,
has the monuments of
the Las Vegas Strip,
and it connects to this backend
agentic sort of server system
that's communicating with
all these different agents.
Do you want to
tell us a bit more
about how that backend
communication works?
And actually, I have
a question here,
which is, what is
an agent exactly?
CASEY WEST: Yeah,
great question.
So I think at its
most basic level--
I'll answer that question first
because that sets the stage
quite well-- at its most basic
level, an agent, I think,
is comprised of
three components.
So we have a model.
In our world these
days, that's usually
a large language model for
producing some sort of text
or generated text.
That text could be anything
from code to narrative.
You have instructions
for the model
to influence it and tell
it what type of job it has,
what role it has, what
the guidelines are.
And then most
importantly, I think,
you have tools, which
is the integrations.
If you imagine anyone doing a
job, the best way to do that job
is to have the right
tools for the job.
And so the model needs
to have good instructions
and good tools.
You put all those things
together and you have an agent.
In our case, we
wanted to envision
what it would look like to
build a large-scale architecture
and what sort of patterns would
emerge when you take something
like simulations, which is a
pretty tried and true piece
of software architecture,
like building simulations is
something we've
done for decades.
But what happens
when it's agentic?
And in our case,
what we learned is
that we need ways for the agents
to collaborate with one another,
discover each other and
what their capabilities are.
We can coordinate
the work, and when
we have a lot of agents, when
we have a lot of sessions
and, in our case, we're
simulating a marathon
with potentially
thousands of runners,
managing those communication
pathways, especially
to the front end,
is really difficult.
So we had to come up with
some new patterns that
tend to model enterprise
solutions pretty well.
TOM GREENAWAY:
Yeah, and developers
will be able to explore the code
and the developer solution we've
created as well, which
showcases how we've
got these different demos that
use different configurations
of agents.
And in those demos, they can
load it up and, in the 3D
frontend, they
can see Las Vegas,
but they can ask an agent
backend, like a planner agent,
to help them plan a marathon
in the city of Las Vegas,
taking into account all the
different sort of stuff that one
would need to take into account
when planning a marathon
in the city.
And that's kind of what we
want to recreate or simulate.
So yeah, it's come
together really well.
Hopefully, it's going to be
exciting at the actual show.
So I have another question
for you, although maybe--
well, I'll do my question,
and you can ask me one.
CASEY WEST: Sure.
TOM GREENAWAY: What are some
of the AI design patterns
that exist that
enterprise developers can
extract from the simulation?
CASEY WEST: Yeah, I think
one of the big things
is how do we get agents to
communicate with one another?
And one of the things
we're working on
at Google and in
Google Cloud are
trying to have standards around
those communication patterns.
So we have an Agent
Development Kit,
which is our primary
framework for building agents.
But then you still need
the agents to communicate
with one another.
We're focused on agent-to-agent
as a protocol, which
is essentially a standard
that allows agents
to advertise their
skills and abilities
and what they're up to.
We use what we call an
agent card for that.
And then you can use anything
from HTTP to HTTP streaming
to communicate.
But also, in our
case, we actually
used essentially a
message bus, which
is, again, a tried and
true enterprise solution.
But we use a message bus
to pass large numbers
of messages with low
latency within the system.
TOM GREENAWAY: Is
that with Pub/Sub?
CASEY WEST: Yes, in this
case, we used Pub/Sub,
and we used Google
Cloud Memorystore, which
is a managed high-scale or
high-availability Redis solution
that we have at Google.
TOM GREENAWAY: Nice.
OK, do you want to
ask me a question?
CASEY WEST: Yeah,
well, so thinking
of design patterns, actually,
and your focus on gaming
and your career, I'm curious
what sort of gaming design
patterns that you
would want to highlight
that we integrated
into the system
or we thought about using?
TOM GREENAWAY: Oh, yeah,
that's a good question.
I mean, there's just a lot of
stuff in the user experience
that we tried to have.
But there's also, in the
backend and the client
and the backend
design, there was
the decision of where
authority of the server was--
sorry, the authority of the
state of the game was held.
So that's always a tricky
one with multiplayer games.
So in our case, we put the game
loop or the majority of the game
loop and that authority of
the state on the server.
Obviously, it's not
a multiplayer game,
but it's a simulation
with many agents.
So there's some kind
of parallels there.
So the client is, we
could say, a dumb client.
It's really just listening to
what's happening on the server.
However, there are certain
events which we did decide made
more sense in the
client, for example,
when it's a bit more precise
and related to the 3D positions
of the objects, like the runners
run along the marathon track,
and we have these kind
of water stations,
which use a 3D sphere to
indicate that they're in this
zone, when they
collide with that,
then it triggers the water
refresh like replenishment
event, which goes
back up to the server,
and that effectively
communicates, I guess,
to an agent that is representing
or connecting with the runners.
And it just gets a message
like, I have drunk some water.
CASEY WEST: That's right.
Yeah, so the backend--
in this case, we're
using an ADK agent
that we called Simulator
that runs a simulation.
And ADK is our framework where
you can have LLM-powered agents,
like I described the
core of an agent--
got models, tools,
and instructions.
But you can also have
deterministic workflows
as part of that
agent architecture.
So we use a looping
agent to loop
through a number
of sampling events.
So when you think about
doing a simulation,
you want to take samples of
data as the simulation occurs.
But that models
very closely to what
we call a game loop in games.
So the server is
essentially running
simulation and advertising
state changes constantly
to the frontend.
But what's nice about the
agentic workflow and the idea
that you have multiple
agents that can all
advertise themselves
and you can communicate
with them independently is
that the front end can also
send events.
What do you call
those in gaming?
TOM GREENAWAY: Oh, an interrupt
or something like that, I mean,
if it's coming from
a different client
to the main state authority.
But it's other interesting
thing I think to highlight,
I guess, and this was
something I didn't realize
at the beginning when we started
to collaborate on this project
and the vision for how the
whole agentic backend would work
is, usually, in projects, you
define some very clear API
endpoints for the client to
be calling to the server.
But actually, the
way we designed this
was to demonstrate how
everything can really just
be almost like a chat message
for the agents to interpret.
CASEY WEST: That's right.
Yeah, the idea with agents,
especially powered by LLMs,
is that you don't have to
be as rigid as you would
be in typical software systems,
where you have to connect APIs,
the APIs are fixed, there
are reference points.
And we still want to have
well-defined APIs and software
architectures.
But with agents,
what we found is
can ask the planner to
run the simulation using
natural language.
You could also ask it by sending
a JSON payload that essentially
represents the same thing.
What's nice is that,
either way, the agent
will interpret it and generally
do the right thing if it
has the right instructions.
TOM GREENAWAY: It's
funny, actually, I just
looked at my next question, and
it's basically what we were just
saying, but it adds on to it.
How steep is the learning
curve to start building
with the A2A protocol
and the agent registry?
CASEY WEST: Yeah,
it's not too bad.
So one of the nice things
on Google Cloud platform,
and especially with Gemini
Enterprise Agent platform,
is that when you deploy your
agents to agent runtime, which
is where you'll typically
want to deploy and run
your agents from,
they get automatically
integrated into
the agent registry,
and they get an agent
card generated for them.
That essentially is the
combination of the A2A protocol
plus the agent runtime
working together.
And so the agent
registry allows us
to have a list of
agents that are
available within
our environment.
And any software system could
query that agent registry
to understand what
agents are available,
including other agents.
TOM GREENAWAY: I mean,
I haven't actually
dived into the
agent registry stuff
that much, but I'm also working
on another project at the moment
where I'm building some
Antigravity skills,
and the skills kind
of need to explain
as well what they're good at
or where they should be used.
So I feel like there's a
similarity there, am I right?
CASEY WEST: Yeah, I think
agent cards actually
can expose the agents skills
as part of the standard.
So the A2A protocol
has that concept.
But skills are basically--
skills are definitely
a new system
that everyone is
adopting across the board
within agentic applications.
They're very popular, and it
means a lot of different things.
This is always the
thing in software
is that we use one
term, and it can
mean a lot of different things.
So in your case,
you're building skills
for an AI or an agenetic
engineering harness,
like Antigravity.
Claude Code uses skills.
Gemini CLI uses skills.
And so, as a
developer, when you're
trying to build something
with AI or AI assistance,
your skills can
help guide the model
to know how to build the
software the way you want it.
Is that how you're using it?
TOM GREENAWAY:
Yeah, that project
will actually be revealed
a bit later in the year.
CASEY WEST: But then
on the cloud side
or on the backend
system side, we're
also integrating
skills into running
agents and autonomous agents so
those agents can have skills.
And that skill is a way to
bundle both instructions
and tools that can be
reused and repurposed
across multiple agents.
TOM GREENAWAY: Cool.
CASEY WEST: So we were
speaking of games quite a bit.
And I think something that's
really fascinating to me--
I'm always looking for the
connections or the patterns that
get repeated.
So we have this client and
server system within gaming,
and I'm not a game developer,
and I don't game a huge amount,
but I see a lot of parallels
to business applications
that we've been building
for the last few years.
We have microservices, which
are distributed systems.
Those are evolving into agents,
which are distributed systems
because we have
multiple agents that
can be deployed independently
and integrated with one another.
And then client
systems, we have things
like data bindings and
Angular as a framework
that can speak to the server.
And when it gets state
updates, it will automatically
refresh the UI.
It feels like it's a lot of
parallels to the way games work.
The game that I'm
most familiar with,
the one that I actually
do play, is "Minecraft"
and I know I'm not
alone-- very popular game.
But it's the same thing.
There's a client and a server.
There's a tick system
or an update system
on the server side.
It sounds very similar.
What do you think?
Do you think that I'm
on the right track?
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah,
funnily enough,
I have not played that
much of "Minecraft."
And I mean, I played it
when it first became--
it started to become popular
and I bought it, I think,
the Java version
at the beginning.
Is that "Minecraft Classic" now?
Is that what it's called?
CASEY WEST: I don't
know what it's called,
but I know that
that's what I play.
I play the Java version.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah,
but I don't actually
know a lot about its
architecture, to be honest.
But I guess you do
run your own server.
And then your friends
can connect to it.
CASEY WEST: You can.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah,
so probably, the server
is the authoritative state.
And I mean, how many users
can it handle, usually?
CASEY WEST: That depends.
So there are a lot of plugins,
and it's a rich ecosystem
for "Minecraft."
So it depends on how much
you optimize your server.
But you could potentially
have hundreds or thousands
of connections.
There's a lot of nuance
there that we probably don't
need to get into in this chat.
But I do think that it's
always interesting to know
how some of the things
that we do for fun
can influence the decisions
we make when we're
building software at work.
And so, for me, I was able
to take some inspiration
in the backend architecture
from my somewhat limited
understanding of how
"Minecraft" works.
But yeah, how about for you?
What sort of games do you play
that might have influenced
how the simulation played out?
TOM GREENAWAY: I don't play
that many games nowadays myself.
But I played lots of
games when I was young.
And I've got some very
specific favorites.
But "Sim City," obviously, was a
game I played back in the '90s.
And when we came up with the
idea for this project, I mean,
it actually took-- there was a
bit of an evolution, actually,
really, because
funnily enough, I
think we said earlier that
you're from the Cloud DevRel.
I'm actually from a team
called Builders DevRel.
And now we're working
together as teams.
And I had worked on,
actually at Google, something
called Adventure, which was a
virtual conference technology we
built during the pandemic.
And we used it for multiple
Google I/Os and other Google
events.
And that had full multiplayer
with characters representing
people, recreating the
physical events but virtually.
And that's how we got
involved working together
was because we were actually
looking at maybe reusing
some of Adventure to do the
agentic simulation experience.
But then as we got closer
to working together,
it sort of made more sense to
make something new and bespoke.
And I remember there was some
initial ideation around like,
oh, maybe it could be like
a "Sim City"-type experience
because we understood that
simulation was going to be
important.
And so then we
had the city idea.
Then I think we changed
to an alien space station,
if I remember correctly.
And then we went back to
a city, and someone else
added this idea
of what if we had
to plan a marathon in a city?
And then we weren't
sure which city to use.
And at one point, I don't
know if you know this,
but someone was asking me a
lot of questions about how does
the marathon in Paris work?
And we were talking
about maybe picking Paris
because there's obviously quite
a few nice monuments there.
But then we just
realized, wait a second,
we're holding the
event in Las Vegas.
Las Vegas has the
whole Las Vegas
Strip with all those monuments.
That's a great place
to try and do it.
So it was just like,
it's really fun,
I think, with projects that have
this creative angle that you
just find your way with them.
CASEY WEST: Yeah, I think
the creative process
of putting together a relatively
ambitious, realistic reference
architecture and
piece of software,
especially being able to open
source it, it's a lot of work.
And we go through a
lot of iterations.
So as you mentioned, we
probably had half a dozen ideas
that we essentially tried to
build out as much as possible
until we landed on
this simulation.
But even within this simulation,
there are some interesting ideas
that some of them made it
in and some of them didn't.
TOM GREENAWAY: That's true.
CASEY WEST: One of our demos
in the developer keynote
is around adding
memory and the ability
to look up especially
unstructured information
within your agent architectures.
So we were integrating the Las
Vegas rules and regulations
in order to understand
what you're allowed to do
and what you're not
allowed to do in Las Vegas
because that can have an impact
on how we plan a marathon,
whether it be the route or
how it might affect traffic
or business impact.
There's an interesting specific
fact about camels that came up.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah, I
never actually looked
into the legislation
or that thing,
but I know that at some point,
we started to talk about putting
like a 3D camel into the
world as one of the runners.
CASEY WEST: Yeah, I can give
you a little insight, which
is one of the laws on the books
in Las Vegas is that you are not
allowed to have a
camel on the road--
specifically a camel
for some reason.
And so, of course, that got
us very interested in camels.
And we really wanted to
put a camel on the road.
TOM GREENAWAY: OK, OK.
And then we were like,
maybe it could just
be a camel emoji at one point.
CASEY WEST: So what
happened with the camel?
TOM GREENAWAY: I don't
remember exactly.
I think that part of the
demo has just ended up,
like, we ran out of time.
We had to reprioritize, which
is sad because RIP camel.
Well, let me see what
else I've got here.
Oh, yeah, which parts of
the game are truly agentic?
What parts have agentic brains?
CASEY WEST: So almost all
of the agents in the system
have an LLM or a
model as a brain,
but that we had to
make some compromises
because a number of reasons.
One of them is that
doing demonstrations
during a one-hour
developer keynote
is a bit of a contrived
experience, in that you have
a very limited amount of time.
So many of us have probably seen
cooking shows, where you prepare
a meal to be baked or
to be put in an oven,
and then it's going to take
hours, potentially in the oven.
So Julia Child was
famous for this.
She'd put something in
the oven and then say,
this has to bake for an hour.
But here, I'll pull this
one out that I've just
completed out of another oven.
And here you go.
Here it is.
And so we do the same
thing a lot in the demos.
But essentially, time
gets really sped up.
So simulations historically
could potentially
run for hours or
days or even longer
because you want as much
information as possible
or because you're modeling
what would be called
an NP-hard problem or
problem that essentially
is an optimization problem
where, at some point,
you have to cut off the
amount of time you compute,
and you just have
to take the best
information you have at that
time to make a decision.
I say all of that to say,
we have planner agents
that are planning a marathon and
planning its impact on the city,
understanding traffic
assessments, that sort of thing.
We have simulator agents.
Those also have LLM brains,
although some pieces
of the simulation are
essentially very deterministic.
For example, we talked
about the game loop.
So when we actually
execute the simulation,
we essentially want to
control time and take
a number of samplings
over an amount of time
that represents the total
duration of a marathon, which
is usually around six
hours for most marathons.
Sometimes, it can be
more, sometimes less,
but about six hours.
And so that's what
we modeled as well.
But I think the real
interesting thing
is where the scale and
complexity starts to play
in with a simulation like this.
The runners themselves,
we wanted to be agentic.
So the runners are agents
in that we use ADK,
we use the Agent
Development Kit.
They speak the A2A protocol,
just all the other agents
in the system.
However, our first
implementation of the runners,
in order to get the
scale we wanted,
actually removed the
LLM from the equation.
So they were deterministic.
And you can think of that
sort of like your classic API.
They took a JSON,
well-structured piece of input.
They manipulated their
state, and then they
reported their new
state back out.
That allowed us to get
subsecond response times out
of the agents.
And then we could have
thousands of them running.
So when we have a tick rate
of every 5 seconds we take
a sample, or every 10
seconds, we take a sample,
we can have 1,000 or even 10,000
runners responding within that
amount of time so that we can
collect our data effectively.
Because as you know from game
development, and I have learned,
is if the tick rates
start to slow down,
that's what we would call lag.
And those of you
who play "Minecraft"
know how problematic
lag is on that game.
And so we didn't want lag.
But we also have a
version of the runners
that is powered by a model.
This is something that I
think is work that's close
to you as well, which is we
wanted a model that we could do
a large number of calls on, but
the runners aren't necessarily
the most intelligent
models out there.
They basically have to
turn their brains off
for the most part and make
very minimal decisions.
But we still want to
represent or understand
what a little bit of
chaos and nondeterminism
would be in a
simulation environment.
So we want the runners to
be able to make decisions
we wouldn't necessarily expect.
So we wanted to use a model.
And so we ended up with an
open-source, open-weight model,
which I think you
have some experience.
TOM GREENAWAY: Yeah, and
my understanding is we're
running that-- the scale
part of that is we're
using Google Kubernetes Engine.
And we're basically
scaling up these Gemma 4
open-weight models.
And I have a question
as well for that.
But I'll come back
to it, I guess.
You're right, I have
been playing around
with Gemma quite a bit lately.
There was another
project I was working on,
which is almost like a
spiritual successor, I guess,
to Adventure.
I've called it, AI
Venture, but it's actually
a little single player vibe
coding puzzle game journey
experience.
But I wanted it
to demonstrate how
Gemma 4 is able to do really
good vibe coding, code
generation locally in that demo.
And also there's actually
a little puzzle--
I don't know if
you saw this one,
but there's one that's
more like an agentic robot
that actually you give
it some instructions,
and it tries to execute over and
over again whatever you tell it.
So yeah, I have been
playing with Gemma 4 lately.
But yeah, I was curious,
with the simulation
in Race Condition, what's the
ratio of runners to Gemma 4
model instances?
CASEY WEST: Yeah,
so a lot of that
is not super easy to
calculate because we
run Gemma 4 on an autoscaling
cluster, a Kubernetes
cluster, or GKE.
And we're running
it using VLLM, which
would be the primary serving
mechanism for a model
these days, especially
on GPUs or TPUs.
So we use VLLM.
And really, the
scaling for the model
itself is about how much
concurrency and token throughput
you can get.
So it's not so much
about how many agents
you're running or agent
sessions you're running.
It's more about how many
tokens do you need to get out
and how many simultaneous
calls do you need to make.
So that calculation is honestly
a little bit challenging.
So in our case, I think
it's around 100 runner
sessions to one VLLM
and Gemma 4 instance.
TOM GREENAWAY: This might
be a silly question,
but I mean, I guess
depending on what's
happening in the simulation,
it would go up and down
how many tokens it needs.
So it's the idea that
GKE can dynamically
scale that appropriately?
CASEY WEST: That's right.
